fixes.explanation: Deer and gazelles never make the list, friend. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, to say the animal comes “…from the herd or the flock.” (Leviticus 1:2) Those two words are the whole menu. Chasing a gazelle across the hills sounds like a very long way to go for a drop-off.

Nice try, but no mountain climbing is needed here. The LORD is speaking from the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 1:1), and that's where the man brings his offering: “…to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting…” (Leviticus 1:3) Mount Sinai isn't named in these instructions. The place that is named is the entrance of that tent.

Yes, friend. The text says, “…Aaron’s sons the priests are to present the blood and splatter it on all sides of the altar at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” (Leviticus 1:5) The man has his own jobs, like slaughtering the young bull before the LORD. The blood belongs to the priests.

The elders aren't mentioned in this part, friend. The job goes to “…Aaron’s sons the priests…” (Leviticus 1:5) The man has plenty to do himself: he slaughters the young bull (Leviticus 1:5), then skins it and cuts it into pieces (Leviticus 1:6). But the blood is handled by the priests.

Moses is the one hearing all of this from the LORD (Leviticus 1:1), but the blood isn't his job. Neither is it Joshua's, and he's Moses's assistant (Exodus 24:13). The text gives it to “…Aaron’s sons the priests…” (Leviticus 1:5) Two big names, and neither one is on the blood crew.

All of it, no leftovers. The animal is skinned and cut into pieces first (Leviticus 1:6), and the entrails and legs are washed. Then the text says, “…the priest shall burn all of it on the altar as a burnt offering…” (Leviticus 1:9) Not one crumb gets set aside.

Only the fat would leave an awful lot behind, friend. For the burnt offering, the text says the priest burns “…all of it…” (Leviticus 1:9) The head and the fat were arranged on the wood with the pieces (Leviticus 1:8). Fat has its own spotlight later, with the peace offering, and that list includes the kidneys and the lobe of the liver too (Leviticus 3:3-4).

Camels? Big personality, but the verse doesn't invite them. The flock is “…the sheep or goats…” (Leviticus 1:10) That's the guest list, and the camel is standing outside the door with a very confident look. Sheep and goats are your two.

You nailed it. The text says, “If, instead, one’s offering to the LORD is a burnt offering of birds, he is to present a turtledove or a young pigeon.” (Leviticus 1:14) So the burnt offering isn't only about bulls and sheep. Birds are on the menu too, and I love that the verse is so specific about which ones.

That's right. The text says, “He shall tear it open by its wings, without dividing the bird completely.” (Leviticus 1:17) So the bird stays in one piece. Then the priest burns it on the altar atop the burning wood.

Correct. The text says, “The remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:3) Aaron's sons are the priests (Leviticus 1:5). The handful goes up in smoke, and the rest is theirs.
Not quite, friend. The text says the remainder “…shall belong to Aaron and his sons…” (Leviticus 2:3) Aaron's sons are the priests (Leviticus 1:5). So the man who brought it doesn't get it back.

There's no next-morning burning in this passage. The text says the remainder “…shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the food offerings to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:3) Aaron's sons are the priests (Leviticus 1:5). The handful is what goes up in smoke.

Barley and water don't show up here, friend. Every version uses fine flour with oil (Leviticus 2:4-7). What changes is how it's made: baked cakes and wafers in the oven, bread on a griddle, or a pan version that says plainly, “…fine flour with oil.” (Leviticus 2:7) Different cookware, but the same two ingredients.

Leaven is one of the two. The text says, “No grain offering that you present to the LORD may be made with leaven, for you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:11) The oven version is described as unleavened cakes and unleavened wafers (Leviticus 2:4). So leaven is a no for these.

Honey is the other one. The verse says, “…you are not to burn any leaven or honey as a food offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:11) Even a guy who stamps cookies all day has to respect that one. Verse 12 adds that they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.

Yes, there's a loophole, and the LORD built it in Himself. The text says, “You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.” (Leviticus 2:12) So leaven and honey can be brought as firstfruits. They just must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.

It's true, friend, and the text spells it out. The verse says, “You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but they must not go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.” (Leviticus 2:12) The word is may, so bringing them as firstfruits is allowed. What they must not do is go up on the altar as a pleasing aroma.

Wine doesn't show up in this offering. The verse says, “…you shall offer crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire.” (Leviticus 2:14) It's grain, crushed and roasted, not flour stirred into a drink. Oil and frankincense are mentioned in the very next verse (Leviticus 2:15).

Both parts are right. The text says, “And you are to put oil and frankincense on it; it is a grain offering.” (Leviticus 2:15) Then, “The priest shall then burn the memorial portion of the crushed grain and the oil, together with all its frankincense, as a food offering to the LORD.” (Leviticus 2:16) So the firstfruits offering gets oil, frankincense and a burned memorial portion.

True, and it's a familiar move. The man lays his hand on the head of the peace offering and slaughters it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 3:2). The burnt offering had that same hand on the head (Leviticus 1:4). Then Aaron's sons the priests splatter the blood on all sides of the altar.

It's true, friend. The text says, “He is to lay his hand on the head of the offering and slaughter it at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting.” (Leviticus 3:2) That matches the burnt offering (Leviticus 1:4). Aaron's sons the priests are the ones who splatter the blood on all sides of the altar.

You got it. The text lists “the fat that covers the entrails, all the fat that is on them, both kidneys with the fat on them near the loins, and the lobe of the liver…” (Leviticus 3:3-4) That's the food offering from the peace offering. Aaron's sons then burn it on the altar atop the burnt offering (Leviticus 3:5).

The head and legs belong to the burnt offering story (Leviticus 1:8-9), not this list. For the peace offering, the text lists “the fat that covers the entrails…” “…both kidneys with the fat on them…” and “…the lobe of the liver…” (Leviticus 3:3-4) The hide isn't on this list. The peace offering has its own parts.

Not for this offering, friend. Even the burnt offering gets skinned before it's burned (Leviticus 1:6). The peace offering's food offering is the fat, the kidneys and the lobe of the liver (Leviticus 3:3-4). Those are the parts that go up on the altar.

Grain is the offering from the chapter before this one, friend. Here the text is on the peace offering, and it says, “All the fat is the LORD’s.” (Leviticus 3:16) The parts that went up on the altar were the fat, kidneys and liver lobe (Leviticus 3:14-15). So the word is fat.
